reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: A malignant tumour of endothelial (vascular or lymphatic) differentiation that can arise in skin, soft tissue, breast, liver, and elsewhere

Cutaneous angiosarcoma of the head and neck in elderly patients is the classic form, often presenting as an ill-defined bruise-like or violaceous plaque that is easily mistaken for benign bruising or infection
Well-recognised secondary forms include radiation-associated angiosarcoma (for example after breast irradiation) and lymphoedema-associated angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome)
Radiation- and lymphoedema-associated cutaneous angiosarcomas frequently show high-level MYC amplification, a useful diagnostic marker
Endothelial markers such as CD31, ERG, and CD34 support the diagnosis, though poorly differentiated tumours can be difficult to recognise
Margins are notoriously difficult to define because of infiltrative, multifocal growth, so wide excision may be combined with radiotherapy
Multi-agent or targeted systemic therapy is often needed given the high propensity for recurrence and metastasis
Overall an aggressive sarcoma with a strong tendency to local recurrence and haematogenous spread, particularly to the lungs
reference.pathophysiology: Angiosarcoma is a malignancy of cells showing endothelial differentiation, forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels or solid sheets in poorly differentiated tumours. It may arise de novo or secondary to chronic lymphoedema, prior radiotherapy, or exposure to certain toxins. Secondary cutaneous forms are characteristically associated with high-level amplification of the MYC oncogene, which drives endothelial proliferation, and additional angiogenic signalling through vascular endothelial growth factor pathways supports tumour growth. Its infiltrative, often multifocal nature reflects diffuse endothelial transformation rather than a single discrete mass, explaining the difficulty in achieving clear margins.
additionalDifferentials: Bruising, haematoma, or cellulitis (for cutaneous lesions)
Poorly differentiated carcinoma or other high-grade sarcoma
additionalInvestigations: MRI or CT of the primary site to assess extent, recognising margins are often underestimated
Whole-body functional imaging in higher-risk disease
Generous, sometimes multiple, biopsies given patchy involvement and diagnostic difficulty
Immunohistochemistry for endothelial markers (CD31, ERG, CD34)
MYC amplification testing by FISH or immunohistochemistry, especially for radiation- or lymphoedema-associated tumours
redFlags: An enlarging or non-resolving bruise-like lesion on the scalp or face of an elderly patient
New skin changes within a previously irradiated field or a chronically lymphoedematous limb
Rapid growth, ulceration, or bleeding of a cutaneous vascular lesion
Haemoperitoneum or hepatic mass raising concern for visceral angiosarcoma
New respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases
reference.prognosis: Angiosarcoma generally carries a poor prognosis with frequent local recurrence and metastasis; outcome depends on site, size, resectability, and patient factors, with large, deep, or metastatic tumours faring worst and even localised disease showing high relapse rates.
pitfalls: Dismissing early cutaneous lesions as bruising, infection, or benign vascular change, delaying diagnosis
Underestimating tumour extent and achieving inadequate surgical margins
Failing to recognise poorly differentiated tumours that mimic carcinoma or other sarcomas without endothelial marker staining
Overlooking a history of prior radiotherapy or chronic lymphoedema that should raise suspicion
Sampling error from a single biopsy of a multifocal or heterogeneous lesion
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Wide surgical excision aiming for clear margins, recognising that infiltrative multifocal growth makes this difficult
Adjuvant or combined radiotherapy to improve local control given frequent positive margins
Taxane chemotherapy such as paclitaxel, or anthracycline such as doxorubicin, for advanced, unresectable or metastatic disease
Antiangiogenic agents such as pazopanib in selected refractory cases, targeting VEGF-driven growth
Staging with cross-sectional imaging of the primary site and chest computed tomography for pulmonary metastases
Close surveillance for local recurrence and metastasis owing to high relapse rates even in localised disease
Management through a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team with early palliative care where appropriate
